items.text: WTI up 1.3% and Brent up 4.0% WoW (to Aug 3), driven by weak China demand and Middle East supply concerns. Energy volatility poses refinancing risks for overleveraged E&P credits; tight spreads currently mask credit stress in commodity-sensitive issuers.

ISM Mfg employment returned to expansion (52.8) for the first time since Jan 2025, signaling genuine labor-market strength, yet July nonfarm payrolls crashed -23K vs. +20K prior. This bifurcation—strong PMI hiring but weak payrolls—suggests data measurement stress or temporary layoff volatility; watch August payrolls and claims for confirmation of structural labor tightening or cyclical roll-over.

Headline CPI fell to 3.46% YoY (June), core to 2.57%, and PCE headline to 3.67% (all June data). One-year inflation expectations eased to 4.2% from 4.6%, but PPI still at 5.51% signals producer-cost stickiness. Disinflation narrative intact but not accelerating; Fed likely on hold at 3.75% for now, keeping long-duration credit at structural disadvantage if growth surprises.

ECB raised deposit facility rate to 2.25% in June. UST 10Y at 4.69% (down 6bps WoW), 2Y at 4.25% (down 3bps), flattening curve to 46bps. Fed funds hold at 3.75%. With Fed on hold and 10Y yields under pressure, refinancing windows are narrowing for sub-investment-grade credits and leverage-heavy sponsors facing 2026–2027 maturities.

HY OAS compressed to 271bps (down 7bps), IG OAS flat at 78bps, CCC OAS widened to 1017bps (+9bps). Spread compression masks deteriorating quality: output growth in manufacturing eased to weakest pace since March while export orders continued to decline amid tariff pressures. Speculative-grade issuers most vulnerable to margin compression from slower growth.

ISM Mfg rose to 55.6 in July, strongest since May 2022, and Services PMI at 54.1, the 25th consecutive month in expansion. Yet China manufacturing PMI fell to 49.2 in July, entering contraction for the first time since February, signaling export demand weakness. GDPNow at 5.83% implies near-term resilience but China's manufacturing pullback and tariff headwinds suggest growth deceleration ahead; credit investors should model margin pressure in growth-sensitive, China-exposed sectors.

University of Michigan consumer sentiment rose to 55.2 in July, a five-month high, but sentiment remains 11% below a year ago. Housing starts rose sharply to 1.43M in June (from 1.20M), but existing home sales fell to 4.09M SAAR from 4.19M. Consumer durables demand remains uneven; housing refinancing waves and consumer leverage stress tests remain key tail risks for subprime-sensitive, retail-backed credit.

themeCards.title: China Manufacturing Contraction
themeCards.statusLine: China manufacturing PMI fell to 49.2 in July, entering contraction for the first time since February, as output, new orders, and foreign orders all turned negative. Decline was driven by persistently weak domestic and external demand, as well as elevated production costs.
themeCards.relevance: Export demand weakness will pressure US corporates with China revenue exposure. Credit investors should stress test issuers with high China capex or supply-chain dependencies; weakness in EM growth could cascade into credit dislocations if capital flows reverse.

themeCards.title: Spread Compression & Quality Deterioration
themeCards.statusLine: HY spreads at 5-month lows (271bps); CCC spreads widened only modestly (1017bps) despite deteriorating fundamentals. Output growth in manufacturing eased to weakest pace since March while export orders continued to decline amid tariff pressures.
themeCards.relevance: Tight spreads obscure credit stress in commodity and tariff-sensitive issuers (autos, industrials, materials). Default risk in lower-rated tranches underpriced; distressed M&A and credit events likely concentrated in BB/B issuers facing margin compression and refinancing walls in 2H 2026.

themeCards.title: Payroll Shock & Labor Data Conflict
themeCards.statusLine: ISM Mfg employment returned to expansion (52.8) for the first time since Jan 2025, yet July nonfarm payrolls fell -23K vs. +20K prior month. Claims inched up to 199K. Labor market bifurcation suggests measurement issues or temporary dynamics.
themeCards.relevance: Conflicting labor signals create uncertainty around Fed policy path and credit cycle momentum. If payroll weakness is structural, consumer leverage and credit card charge-offs could accelerate; if cyclical, near-term credit risk lower but long-term duration risk rises if Fed stays on hold.

themeCards.title: Middle East Supply Disruption
themeCards.statusLine: Sentiment's upward momentum may prove difficult to sustain with more than 70% of interviews completed before the resumption of US strikes against Iran on July 7 and the subsequent reacceleration in gas prices. Energy prices volatile; shipping constraints in Suez region ongoing.
themeCards.relevance: Energy volatility creates refinancing risks for E&P and transportation-dependent credits. Geopolitical risk premium likely to spike again if escalation widens; investors should monitor covenant cushions and hedging adequacy in illiquid credit issuers with Middle East exposure.

themeCards.title: Refinancing Wall & Duration Risk
themeCards.statusLine: UST 10Y at 4.69% (down 6bps WoW); curve flat at 46bps. HY OAS at 5-month lows (271bps) yet CCC at 1017bps. Bond issuance opportunities narrow for lower-rated credits as spreads tighten relative to risk. 2026–2027 maturities loom.
themeCards.relevance: Sub-investment-grade refinancing window is closing. Sponsors with 2027 maturities and weak FCF generation face forced asset sales or equity injections. Special situations investors should screen for refinancing pressure in leveraged buyouts, REITs, and energy credits; high-yield maturity clusters present forced-selling and restructuring opportunities.

regime.detail: Strong services & mfg PMI, but labor shock & China contraction; compressed spreads mask deteriorating fundamentals; refinancing window closing
